deck: 20 Head First Java::07 Better Living in Objectville

cards.front: What is the difference between IS-A and HAS-A?
cards.back: IS-A = inheritance (Dog IS-A Animal); HAS-A = a field reference (Car HAS-A Engine)
cards.extra: IS-A lets a subclass be used where the superclass is expected. HAS-A just holds another object and does not inherit anything — misuse of one for the other is the classic inheritance bug.
cards.example:
class Animal { }
class Engine { }
class Dog extends Animal { Engine e = new Engine(); } // IS-A Animal, HAS-A Engine

cards.front: What does a subclass inherit from its superclass?
cards.back: Public and protected members, plus package-private ones in the same package; private members are inherited but inaccessible, and constructors are not inherited
cards.extra: Inherited methods can be called on the subclass instance as if they were its own. Constructors are not inherited; the subclass calls super(...) instead.
cards.example:
class Animal { public void eat() { } protected void sleep() { } private void hidden() { } }
class Dog extends Animal { void test() { eat(); sleep(); } } // hidden() unavailable; no constructor inherited
class Ex { public static void main(String[] a) { new Dog().eat(); } }

cards.front: A superclass reference holds a subclass object and you call an overridden method. Which version runs?
cards.extra: Animal a = new Dog(); a.makeNoise(); barks. The reference type only decides what you are allowed to call; the object decides what actually runs.
cards.example:
class Animal { void makeNoise() { System.out.println("silence"); } }
class Dog extends Animal { void makeNoise() { System.out.println("woof"); } }
class Ex { public static void main(String[] a) { Animal x = new Dog(); x.makeNoise(); } } // woof

cards.front: Name the three rules a valid override must satisfy.
cards.back: Same name and parameter list; compatible return type; no weaker access modifier
cards.extra: Changing the parameter list turns it into an overload, not an override. Making a public method protected or private in the subclass is a compile error.
cards.example:
class Animal { public Animal make() { return this; } }
class Dog extends Animal { @Override public Dog make() { return this; } } // same args, covariant return, public
// class Bad extends Animal { Animal make() { return this; } } // error: weaker access
class Ex { public static void main(String[] a) { new Dog().make(); } }

cards.front: How does overloading differ from overriding?
cards.back: Overloading = same name, different parameters (declared or inherited), resolved at compile time; overriding = same signature, a subclass replaces the inherited method, dispatched at run time
cards.extra: Overriding = same signature in a subclass, resolved at runtime. Overloads are picked by the compiler from the declared argument types, so the "wrong" one can be chosen for you.
cards.example:
class Animal { void speak(int n) { System.out.println("animal " + n); } }
class Dog extends Animal { void speak(int n) { System.out.println("dog"); } void speak(String s) { } } // override + overload
class Ex { public static void main(String[] a) { Animal x = new Dog(); x.speak(1); } } // dog: runtime

cards.front: Two methods differ only in return type — int get() and long get(). Does that compile?
cards.back: No — return type alone is not a valid overload
cards.extra: The compiler picks an overload from the name and arguments, so it has no way to choose between two identical signatures. Return type is not part of the decision.
cards.example:
class Ex {
    int get() { return 1; }
    // long get() { return 2; } // error: get() is already defined
}

cards.front: Why does polymorphism let you add a new subclass without editing the code that uses the superclass?
cards.back: The calling code only knows the superclass type; the new subclass fits it
cards.extra: A method taking Animal works for any future animal. That is the open/closed idea in practice: new behaviour arrives as a new class, not as an edit to a tested method.
cards.example:
class Animal { void makeNoise() { } }
class Dog extends Animal { void makeNoise() { System.out.println("woof"); } }
class Cat extends Animal { void makeNoise() { System.out.println("meow"); } } // added, caller unchanged
class Ex { public static void main(String[] a) { for (Animal x : new Animal[] {new Dog(), new Cat()}) x.makeNoise(); } }

cards.front: One method must accept a Dog, a Cat and a Lion. What type should its parameter have?
cards.extra: Each subclass IS-A Animal, so one method covers all of them, including subclasses that do not exist yet. This is the practical payoff of inheritance.
cards.example:
class Animal { }
class Dog extends Animal { }
class Cat extends Animal { }
class Lion extends Animal { }
class Ex { static void handle(Animal a) { } public static void main(String[] x) { handle(new Dog()); handle(new Cat()); handle(new Lion()); } }
